rationale: The trial outside Parkinson disease gives a favorable 4.22-point adjusted constipation difference for extra-virgin oil against refined oil. The MEDI-PD analysis includes 36 of 45 randomized participants and gives an inconclusive whole-diet comparison (p=.600). The Parkinson evidence cannot isolate oil grade. The weak favorable lean relies on the active-oil comparison outside Parkinson disease.

Randomized comparisons against water or no snack weakly favor lower anxiety outside Parkinson disease and leave expectancy effects possible. The masked fatigue crossover leaves its paired contrast unresolved. MEDI-PD limits dark chocolate within a whole diet and gives an inconclusive Parkinson anxiety interaction (p=.745). This evidence supports only a weak lean against worsening.

The small Parkinson and non-Parkinson associations use ungraded olive oil and have confounding and multiplicity limits. DieTBra compares active dietary programs, and MEDI-PD's anxiety interaction is inconclusive (p=.745). These programs cannot isolate cold-pressed oil. The minimal favorable lean relies on the earlier observational findings.

Older adults reporting orange consumption had lower unadjusted Rome III constipation prevalence, with preparation unspecified. Pomace trials give mixed stool-frequency results. A pooled-fruit Parkinson survey points the other way on a binary bowel-frequency category. The Lima studies give no orange-specific direction, and the Chagas series combines fruits and physical therapy. The lean against worsening remains minimal. An isolated raw-orange comparison in Parkinson disease remains open.
